sec.title: Background
sec.p: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, characterized by aggressive progression, pronounced stromal desmoplasia, and a limited response to targeted therapies. Although epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors have shown promise in preclinical studies, their clinical efficacy has been modest, suggesting the existence of compensatory signaling networks.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: An integrated analytical framework was employed, combining bulk transcriptomic analyses of TCGA-PDAC and GTEx datasets, DNA methylation profiling, protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, immune infiltration estimation, and single-cell RNA sequencing. Expression patterns and clinical associations of integrin αvβ3 were evaluated using TCGA, GEPIA, UALCAN, and the Human Protein Atlas. Functional validation was performed using in vitro assays in pancreatic cancer cell lines to assess the effects of DL-N2, a tetrac-conjugated nanoparticle targeting integrin αvβ3, alone or in combination with gefitinib.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Integrin αvβ3 (ITGAV/ITGB3) was upregulated in PDAC tissues compared with normal pancreatic tissue and was associated with poor prognosis. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling localized αvβ3 expression to malignant ductal cells and stromal fibroblasts. Computational analyses predicted strong associations of αvβ3 with EGFR, MMP2, and MMP9, implicating it in epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, and immune regulation. In vitro, experiments showed that DL-N2 suppressed basal and EGF-induced proliferation, decreased the expression of EGFR, PCNA, and CCND1, and reduced angiogenic and invasive mediators, including VEGF-α, bFGF2, and MMP9. Notably, DL-N2 inhibited PD-L1 expression, linking αvβ3 signaling to immune evasion. In addition, both DL-N2 and gefitinib inhibited cell migration, and their combined treatment exerted an additive effect on the suppression of pancreatic cancer cell migration.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our findings establish integrin αvβ3 as a multifunctional regulator of pancreatic cancer progression, integrating growth-associated signaling, extracellular matrix regulation, and immune-associated pathways. Targeting αvβ3 with DL-N2 remodels both tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental pathways, potentially enhancing EGFR inhibition and restoring chemosensitivity. Dual blockade of αvβ3 and EGFR represents a rational therapeutic strategy to overcome drug resistance and improve outcomes in PDAC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide. In 2022, approximately 510, 992 new cases were reported globally, with 467, 409 associated deaths [1], A similar trend is observed in Taiwan, PDAC ranks as the 7th leading cause of cancer-related mortality [2]. Due to its asymptomatic nature in early stages, the 5-year survival rate remains a dismal 8% to 13% [3]. As traditional surgery and chemoradiotherapy frequently fail to achieve long-term remission, identifying novel therapeutic targets within the tumor’s complex signaling networks of PDAC remains an important clinical challenge. One such target is the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), which is commonly overexpressed in pancreatic cancer and associated with poor prognosis [4]. However, the efficacy of EGFR-targeted therapies is often limited by the activation of compensatory escape pathways. Emerging evidence suggests that the cell surface receptor integrin αvβ3, which is highly overexpressed in pancreatic cancer cells and the tumor stroma [5], and proliferating endothelial cells, may facilitate this resistance. Beyond its structural role in cell adhesion, integrin αvβ3 functions as the primary membrane receptor for thyroid hormones including triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4) [6]. Binding of these hormones to αvβ3 triggers pro-angiogenic and pro-survival signaling pathways that drive tumor progression and may reduce the efficacy of existing anticancer therapies [7–11].

Critically, the therapeutic potential of targeting integrin αvβ3 is further underscored by its significant crosstalk with EGFR signaling. Previous studies have indicates that thyroid hormone-activated αvβ3 can increase EGFR expression and synergize with epidermal growth factor (EGF) to accelerate cancer cell proliferation [12]. Because both integrin αvβ3 and EGFR signaling converges on the Ras/Raf/ERK signal transduction pathway, they form a redundant survival network that allows tumor cells to bypass single-agent inhibition. Therefore, dual targeting of the thyroxine-αvβ3 axis and EGFR may provide a synergistic approach to disrupt these co-dependent pathways and overcome the therapeutic resistance characteristic of pancreatic cancer.

The first-line therapies of pancreatic cancer include FOLFIRINOX (5-fluorouracil, folinic acid (leucovorin), irinotecan, and oxaliplatin), or gemcitabine/Nab-paclitaxel alone or in association with chemotherapy, as well as target therapies such as EGFR inhibitor, erlotinib, or anti-PD-1 receptor antibody, pembrolizumab or KRAS inhibitors (targeting KRAS G12D or G12V) and PARP inhibitors (like Olaparib for BRCA-mutated cases) [13]. An EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, erlotinib, combined with gemcitabine, demonstrates survival benefits and increases overall survival in the Phase III clinical trial of pancreatic cancer [14]. Phase II studies have shown that nimotuzumab (an anti-EGFR antibody) treatment can achieve significant efficacy in pancreatic cancer patients with high EGFR expression [15]. These findings suggest that combination strategies incorporating EGFR inhibition may provide incremental therapeutic benefit.

Tetraiodothyroacetic acid (Tetrac), a thyroxine deaminated analogue, exhibits anticancer properties that effectively combat various types of cancer cells, including pancreatic cancer cells. It competes with thyroxine for binding to integrins, blocking the downstream signaling pathways, and inhibiting cancer growth and angiogenesis [16–18]. Tetrac and its nanoparticles have shown the ability to reduce the proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells [19]. Tetrac derivatives suppress the activation of EGFR in KRas wild-type cancer cells, resulting in dramatic reductions in both total and phosphorylated EGFR levels in KRas mutant cancer cells [18]. Tetrac nanoparticle (NDAT) alone or in combination with the EGFR inhibitor, gefitinib, overcomes the deficiency of gefitinib to reduce the sialylation of EGFR in K-Ras mutant colorectal cancer cells [20]. In addition, combined treatment with gefitinib and NDAT in K-Ras mutant colorectal cancer cells xenografted mice, NDAT and the combination reduce PD-L1 accumulation and tumor size [20]. On the other hand, gefitinib increases PD-L1 accumulation, which may contribute to resistance to EGFR inhibitors. These studies suggest that targeting integrin αvβ3 by NDAT reduces resistance to EGFR inhibitors, thereby inhibiting cancer growth. Thus, combining tetrac derivatives and EGFR inhibitors may overcome chemotherapy-induced resistance to EGFR inhibitors in pancreatic cancers.

In the current study, we integrated clinical transcriptomic data and in silico analyses to evaluate the pathogenic relevance of integrin αv, integrin β3, and EGFR in PDAC. Multi-omics approaches, including survival, DNA methylation–associated regulation, protein–protein interaction, and immune infiltration analyses, were combined with in vitro validation to establish the functional crosstalk between integrin αvβ3 and EGFR. We employed integrin αvβ3 targeted liposome-conjugated tetrac (DL-N2) either as a single agent or in combination with gefitinib to evaluate its anti-proliferative and anti-metastatic effects in pancreatic cancer cells. Through this integrative approach, our study explores the potential dual targeting of integrin αvβ3 and EGFR targeting as a therapeutic strategy to remodel oncogenic signaling, suppress immune evasion, and enhance drug sensitivity in pancreatic cancer.

sec.title: Data acquisition and preprocessing
sec.p: Publicly available datasets related to Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) were systematically collected and analyzed. Bulk RNA-seq expression and clinical data were obtained from the The Cancer Genome Atlas pancreatic adenocarcinoma cohort (TCGA-PDAC; approximately 170–180 patients). with normal pancreatic tissue data derived from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx), and accessed through GEPIA, UALCAN, and cBioPortal, all of which apply standardized normalization and quality-control pipelines. Patients were stratified into high- and low-expression groups based on median ITGAV or ITGB3 expression for overall survival analyses.

DNA methylation data were retrieved from TCGA-PDAC via MethSurv, immune infiltration estimates were obtained using TIMER and the EPIC algorithm, and protein-level expression data were extracted from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). Single-cell RNA transcriptomic data was obtained from the GSE162708 dataset through the CellXgene platform. This dataset consisted of preprocessed, quality-controlled, and lineage-annotated expression matrices generated by the original authors; no additional filtering or batch correction was applied prior to downstream analysis.

sec.title: Expression of ITGAV and ITGB3 and prognostic relevance in pancreatic cancer
sec.p: Gene expression and survival analyses were conducted using publicly available databases. GEPIA (Gene Expression Profiling Interactive Analysis; http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/) was utilized to assess the differential expression of ITGAV and ITGB3 between pancreatic cancer and normal pancreatic tissues, utilizing TCGA and GTEx data. Expression values were visualized using box plots, and the normality of data distributions was evaluated prior to applying parametric statistical tests. Expression values were visualized using box plots, and the normality of data distributions was assessed prior to applying parametric statistical tests. Statistical significance was determined using GEPIA’s default differential expression model, with multiple testing correction applied, and genes meeting the criteria of |log₂FC| > 1 and adjusted q < 0.01 were considered significant [21]. UALCAN (http://ualcan.path.uab.edu), an interactive portal for TCGA data mining, was utilized to further validate gene expression profiles and investigate their association with clinicopathological parameters, including tumor stage and histological subtype. Transcript per million (TPM) values were used for gene expression comparisons, and for two-group comparisons, Student’s t-test was applied after evaluation of variance homogeneity [22]. In addition, overall survival analysis was performed using Kaplan-Meier plot module in UALCAN, with patients stratifying into high- and low-expression groups based on the median expression levels of ITGAV and ITGB3. Differences in overall survival were assessed using the log-rank test, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant [22].

sec.title: DNA methylation and protein-protein interaction network analysis
sec.p: DNA methylation analysis of ITGAV and ITGB3 was performed using MethSurv (https://biit.cs.ut.ee/methsurv/), utilizing data from the TCGA pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cohort. Methylation β-values at individual CpG sites were compared, and their prognostic relevance was evaluated using univariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis. Hazard ratios (HRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and p values were calculated, and CpG sites with p < 0.05 were considered significant. Heatmaps were generated to visualize methylation patterns across samples [23].

Additionally, to investigate the molecular interactions associated with integrin αvβ3 signaling, a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed using the STRING database (https://string-db.org/). Genes co-expressed with ITGAV and ITGB3 were identified from TCGA-PDAC RNA-seq data. The resulting interaction network was visualized using Cytoscape, highlighting key functional nodes involved in extracellular matrix organization, growth factor signaling, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and immune evasion [24].

sec.title: Immune cell infiltration, clinical datasets, and single-cell transcriptomic profiling of integrin αvβ3 expression
sec.p: To investigate the immunological landscape associated with expression of ITGAV, ITGB3, or EGFR expression with pancreatic cancers, immune cell infiltration analysis was performed using TIMER (https://cistrome.shinyapps.io/timer/) and the EPIC algorithm. Gene expression levels of ITGAV, ITGB3 and EGFR were correlated with the estimated abundance of various tumor-infiltrating immune cells, including B cells, CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells, neutrophils, macrophages, and dendritic cells. Spearman’s correlation test was used to evaluate these associations, and statistically significant relationships (two-sided p-value < 0.05) were visualized using scatter plots [25].

To further validate the expression and localization of integrin αvβ3 in human tissues, immunohistochemistry (IHC) and immunofluorescence data were extracted from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) (https://www.proteinatlas.org/) [26]. Comparisons were made between normal pancreatic tissue and tumor samples to assess the differential expression and subcellular localization of integrin subunits. These findings supported the clinical relevance of integrin αvβ3 in pancreatic tumor biology.

sec.title: Integrin αvβ3 single-cell transcriptomic analysis
sec.p: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data for pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) were obtained from the GSE162708 dataset, accessed through the cellxgene platform (https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/datasets) [27]. The dataset included pre-processed, quality-controlled, and lineage-annotated expression matrices from multiple human PDAC samples, comprising normal pancreatic cells, primary pancreatic tumor cells, and metastatic pancreatic cancer cells as defined in the original dataset annotations. Data analysis was performed using Seurat v5.1.0 in R (v4.4.0). Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis (PCA), followed by Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) for visualizing cellular heterogeneity.

Cell types were annotated based on canonical lineage markers, including epithelial cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, lymphoid cells, and T/NK cells. The expression patterns of ITGAV and ITGB3 were projected onto UMAP/t-SNE plots and quantified using violin plots and heatmaps to assess lineage-specific enrichment. Visualization revealed tumor cell–specific and stromal-associated expression signatures, supporting the predicted role of the αvβ3 integrin complex in the malignant and microenvironmental compartments of PDAC.

sec.title: Gene correlation and pathway enrichment analysis
sec.p: To investigate the functional role of genes associated with integrin signaling in pancreatic cancer, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was performed using RNA-seq data from the TCGA-PDAC cohort [28]. The dataset was retrieved from the Genomic Data Commons (GDC) using the TCGAbiolinks R package. Raw count data were normalized and processed using a limma–voom framework prior to downstream analyses.

For GSEA, samples were stratified into high- and low-expression groups based on median ITGAV or ITGB3 expression levels. Genes were ranked according to differential expression statistics (t-values) derived from limma models, and enrichment analyses were conducted using Hallmark and KEGG gene sets obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB). GSEA was performed in R using the fgsea/clusterProfiler framework with 1,000 permutations. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and pathways with an adjusted false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 were considered statistically significant [29].

Additionally, cBioPortal (https://www.cbioportal.org) was used to identify genes positively correlated with ITGAV and ITGB3 expression in the TCGA PDAC datasets [30]. The top 10% of genes with the highest Pearson correlation coefficients were selected for pathway enrichment analysis. MetaCore (Clarivate Analytics) was employed to identify significantly enriched signaling pathways among the correlated genes. Enrichment results (p < 0.05) were visualized through bar plots and enrichment maps to highlight key signaling cascades associated with integrin-mediated regulation in pancreatic cancer progression and treatment response.

sec.title: Cell lines and culture conditions
sec.p: Human pancreatic cancer cell lines AsPC-1 and BxPC-3 were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA). AsPC-1 cells were derived from nude mouse xenografts established with ascitic fluid from a patient with pancreatic cancer, and BxPC-3 cells were established from a primary PDAC exhibiting epithelial morphology. Cells were maintained in RPMI-1640 (Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco), 1.0 mM sodium pyruvate, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2.

sec.title: Synthesis of DL-N2
sec.p: Tetrac-conjugated liposomes (DL-N2, Taiwan Patent No.: I909106) were synthesized by covalently linking tetraiodothyroacetic acid (tetrac) to DSPE–PEG (1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-polyethylene glycol) and formulating with hydrogenated soy phosphatidylcholine (HSPC) and cholesterol. Liposomes were prepared using the thin-film hydration method followed by extrusion.

sec.title: Quantitative real-time PCR
sec.p: BxPC-3 cells were treated with DL-N2 (10⁻⁷ M), gefitinib (10 µM), or a combination of both for 24 h. All experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates. Total RNA was extracted with genomic DNA removed with an Illustra RNAspin Mini RNA Isolation Kit (GE Healthcare Life Sciences, Buckinghamshire, UK). DNase I-treated total RNA (1 µg) was reverse-transcribed using a RevertAid H Minus First Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Life Technologies) into complementary (c)DNA. cDNAs were used as the template for the real-time PCR and analysis. Real-time PCRs were conducted using a QuantiNovaTM SYBR® Green PCR Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) on a CFX Connect™ Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). The reaction procedure involved initial denaturation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturing at 95 °C for 5 s and combined annealing/extension at 60 °C for 10 s, as shown in detail in the manufacturer’s instructions. Primer sequences are listed in Table 1. The relative gene expression (normalized to 18s reference gene) was calculated according to the ΔΔCT method. The fidelity of the PCR was determined by a melting temperature analysis.

sec.title: Western blot analysis
sec.p: Total cell lysates were prepared after 24 h of treatment. Protein samples (10 µg/lane) were resolved via 10% SDS-PAGE at 100 V and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA). Membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk/TBST (TBS with 0.1% Tween-20) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: p-EGFR (1:1000; Cell Signaling #2236), EGFR (1:2000; GeneTex #GTX628887), PD-L1 (1:1000; GeneTex #GTX104763), p-STAT3-Tyr705 (1:1000; Cell Signaling #9145), STAT3 (1:1000; BD Biosciences #610190), p-ERK1/2 (1:1000; Cell Signaling #4377), ERK1/2 (1:2000; Cell Signaling #9102), and GAPDH (1:20,000; Proteintech #60004-1). After washing with TBST three times for 10 min, membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse (1:20,000; GeneTex #GTX213111-01) or anti-rabbit (1:20,000; GeneTex #GTX213110-01) secondary antibodies. Signals were developed using Immobilon Western Chemiluminescent HRP Substrate (Millipore) and captured via the BioSpectrum Imaging System (UVP, Upland, CA, USA). Band densities were quantified using ImageJ software.

sec.title: Wound healing assay
sec.p: BxPC-3 and AsPC-1 cells were seeded into 12-well plates at a density of approximately 3 × 105 cells per well and cultured until reaching confluence. A vertical scratch was then introduced into the cell monolayer using a 200 µL pipette tip. Following the scratch, the culture medium was replaced with either control medium or medium supplemented with the indicated drugs. At 0, 16, and 24 h post-incubation, images were acquired using an inverted microscope at 100× magnification. The linear migration rate was calculated according to the following formula: Linear Migration Rate = Δ distance / initial distance × 100.

sec.title: Transwell migration assay
sec.p: The migratory capacity of BxPC-3 cells was evaluated using 12‑well Transwell chambers (insert pore size, 8𝜇m; SPL #37224). Briefly, BxPC-3 cells were harvested and resuspended in serum‑free PMI‑1640 medium. A total of 2 × 104 cells were seeded into the upper chamber. The lower chamber was filled with 600 µL of RPMI‑1640 medium supplemented with 10% stripped serum containing DL‑N2, gefitinib, or a combination of both. After 48 h of incubation, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and subsequently stained with 0.5% crystal violet for 15 min. The non‑migrated cells on the upper surface of the membrane were gently removed using a cotton swab. The membranes were then washed with PBS and air‑dried. The images were acquired using an inverted microscope at 100× magnification. The number of migrated cells was determined using ImageJ software. Each experiment was performed in triplicate.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.4.0), GraphPad Prism (version 9; GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA), Microsoft Excel, and ImageJ (version 1.54; National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA). Experimental wet-lab data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent biological experiments. Comparisons between two groups were conducted using a two-tailed Student’s t-test, while analyses involving more than two groups were performed using one-way or two-way ANOVA. Protein band intensity and image-based quantifications were analyzed using ImageJ. Bioinformatic analyses were conducted using publicly available databases and R-based analytical frameworks. Correlation analyses were performed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, and survival analyses were carried out using the Kaplan–Meier method with statistical differences assessed by the log-rank test. For analyses involving multiple hypothesis testing, p-value adjustment was applied to control for false-positive findings. Specifically, false discovery rate (FDR) correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg method for high-dimensional analyses, including differential expression and gene set enrichment analyses, unless otherwise stated. For analysis involving a limited number of comparisons, p-values were not adjusted. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Significance levels are indicated as p < 0.05 (* or #), p < 0.01 (** or ##), and p < 0.001 (*** or ###).

sec.title: Expression patterns of ITGAV and ITGB3 in pancreatic cancer
sec.p: To elucidate the pathogenic relevance of integrin αvβ3 in pancreatic cancer, we first analyzed the transcriptional profiles of its subunits ITGAV (integrin αv) and ITGB3 (integrin β3) across pan-cancer datasets using GEPIA. Both subunits were significantly overexpressed in PDAC tumor tissues compared with normal pancreatic counterparts (p = 0.031) (Fig. 1A–B) [31]. Survival analysis revealed that high ITGAV expression was significantly associated with poor overall survival (p = 0.031), while ITGB3 showed a negative trend that did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.065) (Fig. 1C–D). These findings suggest that ITGAV, and to a lesser extent ITGB3, function as potential oncogenic and prognostic biomarkers in pancreatic cancer [32, 33].

caption.p: ITGAV and ITGB3 are overexpressed in pancreatic cancer and are associated with poor patient prognosis. (A–B) Box plots showing the mRNA expression levels of ITGAV (A) and ITGB3 (B) in Pancreatic tumor tissues (T, n = 179) compared to normal pancreatic tissues (N, n = 171), retrieved from the TCGA database via GEPIA2. Both genes are upregulated in tumor tissues (red boxes) compared to normal (gray boxes); p < 0.05.(C–D) Kaplan–Meier survival analyses from the UALCAN database demonstrating that high expression of ITGAV (C) is significantly associated with reduced overall survival in PAAD patients (p = 0.031), while high ITGB3 expression (D) shows a non-significant trend toward poor survival (p = 0.065). (E–F) DNA methylation heatmaps for ITGAV (E) and ITGB3 (F) illustrating CpG site-specific methylation differences between normal and tumor pancreatic tissues. Tumor samples exhibit increased promoter methylation, particularly in gene regions showing upregulated expression, indicating altered methylation-associated regulation

sec.p: We next explored the DNA methylation–associated regulatory changes of both integrin subunits. MethSurv analysis indicated promoter hypermethylation at multiple CpG sites, including cg07394272 in ITGAV and cg13886698 in ITGB3, in tumor samples relative to normal tissues (Fig. 1E–F). Despite the hypermethylation pattern, both genes remained transcriptionally upregulated, implying non-canonical activation mechanisms, such as enhancer remodeling, transcription factor-driven de-repression, or selective expression in malignant epithelial and stromal compartments. At the protein level, Human Protein Atlas (HPA) immunohistochemistry confirmed strong cytoplasmic and membranous staining of ITGAV and moderate ITGB3 expression in pancreatic tumors, while normal exocrine glandular cells showed minimal signal.

In summary, a clinical big data comparison between normal tissues and pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) indicated that integrin αvβ3 is aberrantly upregulated in PDAC at both the mRNA and protein levels, suggesting that integrin signaling may play a vital role in the pathogenesis of PDAC.

sec.title: Integrin αvβ3 marks an immune-infiltrated, myeloid-enriched tumor microenvironment in PDAC
sec.p: To characterize the immune and cellular landscape associated with integrin αvβ3 in PDAC, we first analyzed the correlation and immune infiltration using the TIMER2.0 database (Supplementary Fig. S). Both ITGAV and ITGB3 expression levels showed strong positive associations with infiltrating CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells, indicating that αvβ3-expressing tumors attract a large population of immune cells. However, this apparent immune-rich phenotype is deceptive, as the dominance of myeloid cells such as tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and neutrophils indicates a functionally immunosuppressive microenvironment. These cell types are known to release TGF-β, IL-10, and matrix metalloproteinases (MMP2 and MMP9), which degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM), suppress T-cell activation, and promote tumor invasion and angiogenesis. B cell infiltration was moderate, while CD4⁺ helper T cells exhibited weak or nonsignificant correlations, underscoring a selective recruitment pattern that favors myeloid infiltration over adaptive immunity. This pattern reflects the biological hallmark of PDAC, an immune-excluded or cold tumor phenotype where chronic inflammation and desmoplastic stroma coexist with poor cytotoxic immune activity. Thus, αvβ3 likely functions not merely as an adhesion receptor but as a microenvironmental switch that integrates mechanical and cytokine signals to reprogram immune cell composition toward an immunosuppressive state, promoting tumor persistence.

To determine the cellular origins of αvβ3 expression, we next analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from human pancreatic cancer tissues (GSE162708) (Fig. 2). In this dataset, normal cells are derived from non-malignant pancreatic tissue, primary tumor cells originate from pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma lesions, and metastatic cells represent pancreatic cancer metastases as defined by the original dataset annotations. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) projections revealed that both ITGAV and ITGB3 are preferentially expressed in malignant ductal clusters and stromal fibroblasts, whereas their expression was nearly absent in normal acinar, endocrine, or peripheral immune compartments. Quantitative subset analysis revealed that ITGAV is markedly upregulated in metastatic (37.01%) and primary tumor clusters (30.29%), whereas it remains low in normal pancreatic and PBMC-derived cells. ITGB3 exhibited a similar, though more restricted, expression pattern, confined mainly to malignant epithelial cells and metastatic niches. This selective induction of integrin αvβ3 in tumor and stromal lineages suggests a tumor-specific activation program driven by oncogenic stress, extracellular matrix stiffness, and paracrine growth factors such as TGF-β and EGF, each of which can transcriptionally upregulate integrins through the FAK–Src–MAPK pathway.

sec.p: Further Violin-plot analysis (Fig. 3) confirmed the compartmentalized expression of integrin subunits across key cellular lineages. ITGAV displayed broad distribution across malignant epithelial cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, and endothelial cells, reflecting its function as a structural anchor and signaling conduit during tumor growth and fibrosis. In contrast, ITGB3 expression was enriched primarily within myofibroblasts and macrophage-like stromal populations, supporting its role in matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, and the formation of the immunosuppressive niche. Together, these results indicate that αvβ3 is not ubiquitously expressed across the pancreas but instead becomes reactivated in malignant and desmoplastic contexts, where it drives reciprocal signaling between epithelial cancer cells and stromal fibroblasts. Together, these results indicate that integrin αvβ3 expression is compartmentalized within malignant and stromal populations, consistent with its reported roles in extracellular matrix organization and cell–stroma interactions in PDAC.

(C–D) Violin plots regrouped by functional category (immune, stromal, and malignant compartments) further highlight selective enrichment of ITGAV in stromal and malignant cell clusters, with comparatively lower expression of ITGB3, suggesting complementary but nonredundant roles of integrin αvβ3 subunits in tumor–stroma crosstalk

sec.p: Integrating the TIMER and single-cell analyses reveals a consistent association between integrin αvβ3, which marks a highly remodeled, immune-modulated tumor ecosystem. Its expression across both tumor and stromal compartments is associated with signaling pathways linked to cell proliferation and immune regulation, including EGFR/FAK–ERK signaling and markers of myeloid-enriched immune infiltration. Mechanistically, integrin αvβ3 activation amplifies downstream ERK and PI3K/AKT signaling, upregulates cytokines such as IL-6 and VEGF, and stabilizes PD-L1 on the tumor surface, collectively fostering a microenvironment resistant to immune attack and chemotherapy. This dual role explains why integrin αvβ3 blockade using DL-N2 nanoparticles produces multifaceted therapeutic effects: it directly inhibits integrin-mediated tumor signaling while simultaneously disrupting the crosstalk between cancer cells, fibroblasts, and infiltrating immune cells.

Taken together, these results identify integrin αvβ3 as a central organizer of the pancreatic tumor microenvironment, coupling malignant epithelial signaling with stromal activation and immune suppression. The combined TIMER and single-cell evidence underscore αvβ3’s clinical importance not only as a biomarker of tumor aggressiveness but also as a mechanistically actionable target. Targeting αvβ3 with DL-N2 offers a biologically grounded strategy to dismantle the fibro-immune network, normalize the microenvironment, and restore therapeutic sensitivity in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

sec.title: Functional enrichment analysis of ITGAV and ITGB3 reveals key signaling pathways in PDAC
sec.p: To gain a deeper understanding of the biological programs orchestrated by integrin αvβ3 in pancreatic cancer, we first conducted GSEA on genes positively correlated with ITGAV and ITGB3 in TCGA-PDAC (Fig. 4A-B). For both subunits, enrichment was observed in hallmark pathways that strongly reinforce the proposed mechanistic model and therapeutic implications of targeting integrin αvβ3. Notably, Epithelial–Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) emerged as a top enriched pathway in both ITGAV- and ITGB3-associated gene sets, supporting our hypothesis that integrin αvβ3 drives cellular plasticity, migration, and invasion in PDAC (Fig. 5A). This is consistent with our protein–protein interaction analysis that links integrins to key EMT regulators such as SNAI1, ZEB1, and TWIST1, and with prior evidence showing integrin-mediated activation of FAK and PI3K/AKT signaling, which promotes EMT. Enrichment of the mTORC1 signaling pathway in both integrin profiles further supports the integrin–EGFR axis, given that mTORC1 is a known downstream effector of EGFR and integrin co-signaling. This complements our in vitro findings, where DL-N2, an integrin-targeting agent, downregulated EGFR and proliferation-associated genes, such as CCND1 and PCNA, and may enhance the anti-proliferative effects of the EGFR inhibitor gefitinib.

Bar plot shows the top 10 enriched biological pathways associated with ITGAV expression in TCGA-PAAD. Significance is represented as -log(p-value) on the x-axis. ITGAV-associated genes are enriched in pathways related to epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, and TGF-β-mediated fibroblast migration, processes central to tumor invasion and fibrosis. Several pathways, including tumor–stroma interactions, stellate cell activation, and cytoskeleton remodeling, overlap with EGFR signaling cascades, suggesting cooperative roles of ITGAV and EGFR in promoting pancreatic cancer progression

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of ITGAV and ITGB3-associated transcriptomes in pancreatic cancer. (A) GSEA of ITGAV-high vs. ITGAV-low expression groups revealed significant enrichment of hallmark gene sets related to glycolysis, apoptosis, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), inflammatory response, KRAS signaling, and hypoxia. Representative enrichment plots highlight apoptosis and EMT pathways. (B) GSEA of ITGB3-high vs. ITGB3-low expression groups demonstrated enrichment in hallmark gene sets including TNFα signaling via NF-κB, apoptosis, EMT, KRAS signaling, inflammatory response, and angiogenesis. Representative enrichment plots show EMT and apoptosis pathways. Together, these findings suggest that ITGAV and ITGB3 converge on shared oncogenic programs that promote tumor progression and resistance mechanisms in pancreatic cancer

sec.p: In addition, Apoptosis was observed to be enriched in both ITGAV and ITGB3 signatures, suggesting that high integrin αvβ3 expression may suppress apoptosis and confer survival advantages to tumor cells. This mechanistically aligns with our data, which show that DL-N2 treatment may enhance cell death and augment gefitinib-induced apoptosis in pancreatic cancer cells. Intriguingly, DNA repair pathways were enriched in the ITGAV gene set, suggesting a potential link between integrin signaling and genomic stability. Integrin αv is known to facilitate survival under genotoxic stress, which may contribute to resistance to conventional therapies, underscoring the relevance of targeting integrins to overcome this resistance.

Notably, ITGB3-specific enrichment of the Interferon Gamma Response and Inflammatory Response pathways underscores its role in immune modulation (Fig. 5B). These pathways are associated with immune cell recruitment, cytokine signaling, and immune evasion, which resonates with our observations that DL-N2 reduces PD-L1 expression and correlates with increased infiltration of CD8⁺ T cells and macrophages, as shown in TIMER analysis. Altogether, these GSEA findings offer functional insight into how ITGAV and ITGB3 coordinate pro-oncogenic programs encompassing EMT, proliferation, apoptosis resistance, and immune suppression. These results substantiate integrin αvβ3 as a central node in pancreatic cancer progression and therapeutic resistance and strongly support our rationale for targeting this integrin complex using DL-N2 in combination with EGFR inhibitors to improve therapeutic outcomes.

sec.title: MetaCore pathway enrichment reveals integrin αvβ3-Driven EMT, ECM Remodeling, and crosstalk with EGFR signaling in PDAC
sec.p: To further dissect the downstream signaling networks and gain deeper mechanistic insights, we performed MetaCore pathway enrichment analysis on ITGAV and ITGB3 correlated genes in TCGA-PDAC. This analysis revealed significant enrichment in pathways associated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, cytoskeletal reorganization, and TGF-β signaling (Figs. 4 and 6A-B; Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). These processes are central to PDAC progression, contributing to tumor invasion, metastasis, and chemoresistance [34, 35]. Importantly, the extended pathway enrichment maps are provided in Supplementary Figs. 2–5 for ITGAV and Supplementary Figs. 6–10 for ITGB3, offering a detailed visualization of the signaling cascades.

caption.p: Pathway enrichment analysis of ITGB3-associated genes highlights EMT, fibroblast activation, and EGFR pathway crosstalk. Bar plot shows the top 10 enriched biological pathways associated with ITGB3 expression in TCGA-PAAD. Significance is represented as -log(p-value) on the x-axis. ITGB3-associated genes are enriched in EMT, ECM remodeling, and TGF-β-driven fibroblast migration pathways that contribute to desmoplasia and metastasis. Enriched pathways related to stellate cell activation, cytoskeleton reorganization, and tumor–stroma signaling also align with EGFR-linked oncogenic processes, indicating integrin–EGFR pathway synergy within the pancreatic tumor microenvironment

sec.p: Integrin αvβ3 promotes EMT and cancer cell motility through activation of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and downstream PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK signaling cascades [36, 37]. Notably, several of the enriched integrin-related pathways overlap with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-linked signaling, including the Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR axes, indicating potential synergistic or compensatory interactions between integrin and EGFR pathways in PDAC. Integrin αvβ3 can directly interact with EGFR at the plasma membrane, facilitating ligand-dependent and independent receptor activation, nuclear translocation, and prolonged downstream signaling, all of which enhance tumor proliferation and invasion [31]. Moreover, integrin activation in stiff ECM environments, a characteristic feature of pancreatic tumors, has been shown to mechanically induce EGFR activation, promoting immune evasion through upregulation of PD-L1 [38]. The presence of TGF-β and cytoskeletal remodeling signatures further implicates integrin αvβ3 in tumor–stroma interactions, desmoplasia, and fibroblast activation, all of which contribute to immune suppression and drug resistance [39]. These computational findings provide a strong rationale for targeting integrin αvβ3 to disrupt pro-oncogenic EGFR signaling, remodel the tumor microenvironment, and enhance the sensitivity of tumors to EGFR inhibitors. Our experimental results showing enhanced anti-proliferative effects of DL-N2 in combination with gefitinib are consistent with this model and support the therapeutic potential of dual inhibition of integrin αvβ3 and EGFR in pancreatic cancer.

sec.title: Integrin αvβ3 establishes functional crosstalk with EGFR and matrix remodeling enzymes in PDAC
sec.p: To gain mechanistic insight into the signaling context of integrin αvβ3, we explored PPI networks and gene expression correlations of ITGAV and ITGB3 in PDAC. STRING-derived analysis (Fig. 7A) revealed that ITGAV and ITGB3 occupy central network positions, connecting with multiple oncogenic regulators, including EGFR, FN1, CD44, STAT3, and EMT-related transcription factors such as ZEB1, TWIST1, and SNAI2. Among the strongest predicted interactions were those between ITGAV and ITGB3 themselves (node score = 0.999), confirming the stability of the αvβ3 heterodimer, as well as between ITGAV and EGFR (score = 0.686) and between ITGB3 and EGFR (score = 0.650). These high-confidence interactions suggest that αvβ3 forms a functional axis with EGFR, reinforcing downstream oncogenic signaling cascades.

sec.p: Expression-based correlation analysis further supported this association. Using TCGA-PDAC datasets, both ITGAV and ITGB3 displayed significant positive correlations with EGFR mRNA levels (Fig. 8B–C), with Spearman correlation coefficients of R = 0.48 (p = 9.2 × 10⁻¹²) for ITGAV–EGFR and R = 0.31 (p = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵) for ITGB3–EGFR. Similarly, Supplementary Fig. S11 demonstrated robust co-expression patterns among ITGAV, ITGB3, and EGFR, with Pearson correlation coefficients ranging from 0.44 to 0.61. These findings collectively highlight an αvβ3–EGFR co-activation module in pancreatic cancer, consistent with prior reports showing that integrin β3 facilitates EGFR clustering and ligand-independent activation in solid tumors [40, 41]. Such crosstalk not only amplifies proliferative ERK/AKT pathways but also promotes resistance to EGFR-targeted therapies.

caption.p: Protein–protein interaction network and correlation of ITGAV and ITGB3 with EGFR expression.(A) Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network of ITGAV and ITGB3 and their associated genes, generated using the STRING database. The network illustrates key predicted interactions involved in cell adhesion, migration, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT). Table listing interaction scores between ITGAV/ITGB3 and selected partner genes, highlighting strong associations with EGFR (interaction score > 0.6 for both). (B–C) Correlation analysis using GEPIA shows a significant positive correlation between EGFR expression and ITGAV (B) as well as EGFR and ITGB3 (C) in PAAD samples. Spearman correlation coefficients and p-values are indicated, supporting a functional association between integrin αvβ3 subunits and EGFR signaling in pancreatic cancer

sec.p: Beyond growth factor signaling, αvβ3 also displayed functional connections with extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling enzymes. Supplementary Fig. S12 illustrates that ITGAV and ITGB3 were highly associated with MMP2 (ITGAV–MMP2 score = 0.835; ITGB3–MMP2 score = 0.588) and MMP9 (ITGB3–MMP9 score = 0.543; ITGAV–MMP9 score = 0.494). Correlation heatmaps further validated these associations, with ITGAV expression showing positive relationships with MMP2 (r = 0.69) and ITGB3 with MMP9 (r = 0.43). Biologically, this axis reflects the established role of integrins in promoting ECM degradation, invasion, and metastasis through the recruitment of MMP activity at the tumor–stroma interface [42–45]. In pancreatic cancer, MMP2 and MMP9 have been implicated in the development of desmoplasia, chemoresistance, and the formation of an immunosuppressive niche, suggesting that αvβ3-driven MMP regulation is a critical driver of tumor progression.

Taken together, these findings establish a tripartite interaction between integrin αvβ3, EGFR, and matrix metalloproteinases in PDAC. By coupling growth factor receptor signaling with ECM remodeling machinery, αvβ3 not only sustains proliferative and survival pathways but also promotes invasion and stromal reprogramming. This dual role positions αvβ3 at the intersection of oncogenic signaling and microenvironmental remodeling, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target to disrupt tumor growth, desmoplasia, and metastasis in pancreatic cancer.

sec.title: Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescent validation of ITGAV and ITGB3 expression and their functional association with EGFR
sec.p: To experimentally validate the predicted ITGAV–ITGB3–EGFR interaction network derived from our MetaCore and STRING PPI analyses, we examined integrin αvβ3 protein expression and localization in human pancreatic tissues and model cells (Fig. 7A-C). IHC images from the Human Protein Atlas revealed that both ITGAV (antibody HPA004856) and ITGB3 (antibody HPA028463) are markedly upregulated in PDAC tissues compared with the normal pancreas. Normal exocrine cells showed weak or undetectable staining, whereas tumor sections displayed strong cytoplasmic and membranous expression, consistent with active integrin signaling at the plasma membrane. Quantitative summary charts of all available HPA samples (ITGAV n = 12; ITGB3 n = 10) indicated that high-to-medium staining frequencies dominate in tumor tissues, while normal samples remain largely negative (Fig. 7D-E).

To further validate the subcellular distribution and potential interaction with EGFR, we examined immunofluorescence (IF) data of A431 cells available in the HPA database (Supplementary Fig. S13A-B). A431 cells, a human epidermoid carcinoma line that endogenously co-expresses high levels of EGFR and αvβ3 integrin. A431 cells were strategically selected for their flat morphology, strong surface receptor abundance, and well-defined EGFR signaling, which together enable high-resolution visualization of receptor organization that is technically challenging in pancreatic cancer cells due to their compact, granular cytoplasm. IF imaging revealed distinct membrane localization of ITGAV and partial cytoplasmic and perinuclear distribution of ITGB3, consistent with dynamic αvβ3 heterodimerization, internalization, and recycling features characteristic of active integrin complexes engaged in receptor crosstalk. Merged channel visualization showed close spatial overlap of αvβ3 and EGFR signals, validating the physical proximity and cooperative interaction predicted in silico.

Biologically, these findings confirm that integrin αvβ3 not only acts as a structural adhesion receptor but also functions as a co-receptor for EGFR, creating a signaling platform that amplifies downstream ERK1/2 and PI3K/AKT activation. This interaction may enhance anchorage-dependent growth, survival under stress, and migration, key hallmarks of pancreatic tumor aggressiveness. The A431-based IF model therefore provides crucial mechanistic evidence that αvβ3 can directly interface with EGFR to potentiate oncogenic signaling, supporting the concept that the αvβ3–EGFR complex serves as a driver of proliferative and immune-evasive phenotypes in PDAC.

sec.title: Targeting integrin αvβ3 by antagonist suppresses EGFR-dependent cancer progression in pancreatic cancer cells
sec.p: Our computational analyses suggested that integrin αvβ3 (ITGAV/ITGB3) may act as a central hub linking extracellular matrix signaling to EGFR-driven PDAC progression. To validate this prediction, we investigated the effects of DL-N2, a tetrac nano-derivative, which competes with thyroxine targeting the integrin αvβ3 RGD binding domain. DL-N2 (10⁻⁹–10⁻⁷ M, 72 h) significantly inhibited basal proliferation of BxPC-3 and AsPC-1 cells in a dose-dependent manner (Figs. 9A and B), confirming that integrin αvβ3 provides a constitutively proliferative signal in PDAC. Meanwhile, DN-N2 suppressed 100 ng/mL EGF-induced cell proliferation (Fig. 9B), indicating that integrin αvβ3 blockade interferes with EGFR-mediated mitogenic signaling. We further investigated the effects of DL-N2 and gefitinib, an EGFR inhibitor, on pancreatic cancer cells. The results demonstrated that combined treatment with DL-N2 and gefitinib more effectively suppressed cancer cell growth both in BxPC-3 and AsPC-1 cells (Fig. 9C–D). We next examined the effects of DL-N2 and gefitinib on gene expression in pancreatic cancer cells. In BxPC-3 cells, DL-N2 downregulated the mRNA levels of EGFR, PD-L1, and PCNA, while its combination with gefitinib further suppressed the expression of EGFR, PD-L1, CCND1, and PCNA (Fig. 10A-D). Conversely, although DL-N2 monotherapy induced an opposing response in AsPC-1 cells, the combination therapy reversed this trend, significantly inhibiting the expression of EGFR, PD-L1, and PCNA (Fig. 10E-H).

sec.title: DL-N2 attenuates invasion- and angiogenesis-associated signaling through the integrin αvβ3-MMP axis
sec.p: Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of DL-N2 on the expression of genes associated with matrix remodeling and angiogenesis. In BxPC-3 cells, DL-N2 treatment was associated with reduced expression of the metastasis-associated gene MMP9 and suppressed the pro-angiogenic factors bFGF2 and VEGF-α. In AsPC-1 cells, DL-N2 treatment also reduced MMP9 expression; monotherapy with either DL-N2 or gefitinib upregulated bFGF2 and VEGF-α. Notably, their combined treatment reversed this effect (Fig. 11). This suggests that blockade of αvβ3 not only restrains growth but also prevents compensatory activation of pro-angiogenic and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling pathways that typically emerge following EGFR inhibition.

sec.title: DL-N2 and gefitinib synergistically inhibit integrin αvβ3–EGFR–ERK signaling and downstream immune modulators in pancreatic cancer cells
sec.p: We next investigated the effects of DL-N2 and gefitinib on the αvβ3–EGFR–ERK signaling pathway. DL-N2 reduced EGFR activation but increased pSTAT3 protein expression, whereas gefitinib alone decreased the levels of pEGFR and pERK1/2 (Fig. 12).

sec.p: DL-N2 alone markedly reduced phosphorylated EGFR levels, indicating that integrin αvβ3 acts as a structural scaffold stabilizing EGFR at the plasma membrane and facilitating its recycling and ligand-independent activation. Disruption of this integrin-EGFR complex by DL-N2 destabilizes receptor homeostasis, leading to attenuation of downstream Ras–Raf–MEK–ERK signaling. Gefitinib monotherapy reduced p-EGFR but not total EGFR, consistent with its catalytic-site inhibition. Notably, the combination of DL-N2 and gefitinib nearly abolished both total and phosphorylated EGFR. Downstream, co-treatment markedly suppressed phospho-ERK1/2, confirming blockade of the MAPK pathway.

sec.title: DL-N2 and gefitinib cooperatively suppressed cell migration through integrin αvβ3–EGFR targeting
sec.p: In addition to gene expression analyses, we further evaluated the effects of DL-N2 and gefitinib on the migratory capacity of pancreatic cancer cells using a wound healing assay. The results showed that both DL-N2 and gefitinib significantly inhibited cell migration in BxPC-3 and AsPC-1 cells at 16 h and 24 h. Notably, the combination of DL-N2 with gefitinib exerted a more substantial inhibitory effect on cell migration (Fig. 13). To further substantiate these findings, a Transwell migration assay was conducted using BxPC‑3 cells, which carry a KRAS mutation. In line with the wound healing assay, treatment with either DL‑N2 or gefitinib significantly reduced the number of migrated cells compared with the control group. Notably, the combination therapy produced a more pronounced inhibition of cell migration, underscoring its superior efficacy relative to monotherapy (Fig. 14).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest malignancies due to its late presentation, aggressive biology, and limited therapeutic responses. Despite the development of EGFR inhibitors, clinical benefit remains modest, reflecting a key therapeutic gap: the lack of effective strategies to overcome resistance and simultaneously target both oncogenic signaling and the tumor microenvironment.

Integrin αvβ3 is a structural plasma membrane protein that mediates extracellular matrix–cell interactions and has been repeatedly implicated in cancer pathogenesis. Previous studies have reported that integrin αvβ3 enhances pancreatic tumor progression and metastasis [46, 47]. Thyroxine, a thyroid hormone, can stimulate cancer cell proliferation through direct binding to the cell surface receptor integrin αvβ3, thereby activating downstream signal transduction cascades. The thyroxine–αvβ3 axis has been shown to play a crucial role in the progression of multiple malignancies, including pancreatic cancer [9–11].

Clinical transcriptomic datasets demonstrated that ITGAV and ITGB3, the subunits of αvβ3, are overexpressed in pancreatic cancer cells compared with normal pancreatic tissues. High ITGAV expression correlated with worse overall survival, while single-cell transcriptomic mapping localized both subunits to malignant ductal clusters and stromal fibroblasts, but not to normal acinar or endocrine cells. This tumor-specific induction suggests that αvβ3 is not a generic adhesion receptor but rather a malignancy-associated integrin that provides selective advantages in the tumor ecosystem. These findings are consistent with recent studies showing that αvβ3 is enriched in aggressive solid tumors and is associated with a poor prognosis [48, 49]. Biologically, this overexpression enhances cell adhesion to extracellular-matrix ligands (vitronectin, fibronectin, laminin), promotes FAK–Src–Ras–ERK activation, and cooperates with EGFR to sustain proliferative and survival signaling. The elevated αvβ3 complex also facilitates interactions with tumor-associated fibroblasts and immune cells, reinforcing a pro-invasive and immunomodulatory microenvironment. Collectively, the data highlight ITGAV/ITGB3 as central molecular nodes that link extracellular matrix remodeling, growth factor signaling, and immune evasion in pancreatic cancer.

To clarify the biological programs coordinated by αvβ3, we performed enrichment and protein–protein interaction analyses. Genes co-expressed with ITGAV and ITGB3 were upregulated in hallmark pathways related to epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), ECM remodeling, and growth factor signaling. PPI networks placed αvβ3 in close functional proximity to EGFR and matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP2 and MMP9, suggesting that it integrates growth-associated signaling with invasive capacity. Our experimental validation directly confirmed these computational predictions: DL-N2 treatment downregulated MMP9, VEGF-α, and bFGF2, thereby suppressing both invasion and angiogenesis [50]. This consistency between in silico analysis modeling and experimental data underscores the biological robustness of αvβ3 as a regulator of both tumor expansion and stromal remodeling.

Confirming the synergistic degradation of the integrin-anchored receptor complex and validating the PPI network prediction that ITGAV/ITGB3 physically anchors EGFR to sustain mitogenic signaling. Downstream, co-treatment markedly suppressed phospho-ERK1/2 while leaving total ERK unchanged, confirming blockade of the MAPK pathway. This suppression aligns with GSEA and MetaCore enrichment for the “ERK-dependent proliferation” and “MAPK-fibrosis” pathways. It is supported by prior qPCR data showing reduced expression of CCND1 and PCNA under similar conditions. Together, these data indicate that dual αvβ3–EGFR inhibition converts a proliferative signaling landscape into a quiescent phenotype.

Our in-silico studies indicated that biologically, these findings confirm that integrin αvβ3 not only acts as a structural adhesion receptor but also functions as a co-receptor for EGFR, creating a signaling platform that amplifies downstream ERK1/2 and PI3K/AKT activation. This interaction may enhance anchorage-dependent growth, survival under stress, and migration, key hallmarks of pancreatic tumor aggressiveness. The A431-based IF model therefore provides crucial mechanistic evidence that αvβ3 can directly interface with EGFR to potentiate oncogenic signaling, supporting the concept that the αvβ3–EGFR complex serves as a driver of proliferative and immune-evasive phenotypes in PDAC.

In vitro results indicated that integrin αvβ3 modulated EGFR-dependent cancer progression in pancreatic cancer cells (Fig. 6), which are consistent with our in-silico analysis observations. ITGAV/ITGB3 exhibit high interaction scores with EGFR in protein–protein interaction networks (STRING scores of 0.686 for ITGAV–EGFR and 0.650 for ITGB3–EGFR). Additionally, they correlate positively with EGFR expression in TCGA-PDAC cohorts. Mechanistically, this aligns with previous reports showing that integrin β3 stabilizes EGFR signaling by sustaining FAK–Src–ERK/PI3K–AKT pathways and mediating resistance to EGFR blockade [51, 52].
In addition, DL-N2 has been shown to downregulate proliferative and immune-evasive mediators, including, and to modulate these pathways, linking these findings to broader tumor progression networks.

In parallel, immune checkpoint signaling via programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and its ligand PD-L1 plays a crucial role in tumor immune evasion, allowing cancer cells to escape destruction by cytotoxic T cells [53–55]. Increased PD-L1 expression strongly correlates with aggressive tumor progression. Our recent studies have demonstrated that thyroxine can induce PD-L1 expression and protein accumulation in colorectal cancer cells [56], breast cancer cells [56], and oral cancer cells [56]. The expressed PD-L1 translocates to the nucleus and involves gene regulation [57, 58]. The role of PD-L1 is not limited to immunomodulation. Beyond its role in T-cell suppression, PD-L1 is now recognized to regulate several non-immune processes in cancer cells. High PD-L1 expression is linked to increased N-cadherin and Vimentin, promoting cell motility and invasion. PD-L1 maintains the self-renewal of cancer stem cells (CSCs) by activating pathways, such as the PI3K/AKT pathway, and regulating transcription factors like Oct4 and Nanog [59].

DL-N2 suppressed PD-L1 expression (Fig. 10) and nearly eliminated it under combination treatment. These results indicated that crosstalk between EGFR and integrin αvβ3. When blocking integrin αvβ3 and interfering with EGFR activity with gefitinib, it inhibited PD-L1 expression collaboratively. This trend aligns with TIMER2.0 and TCGA-PDAC correlations, which show positive associations between ITGAV/ITGB3 and CD274 (PD-L1). Mechanistically, αvβ3–EGFR signaling activates ERK1/2 and STAT3, which cooperate to drive PD-L1 transcription through AP-1 and STAT response elements. Thus, DL-N2 combined with gefitinib co-treatment dismantles this transcriptional machinery, restoring an immune-permissive state by reversing ERK- and STAT3-driven PD-L1 induction. Taken together, these results demonstrate that integrin αvβ3 sustains EGFR activity, promotes downstream ERK signaling, and contributes to the upregulation of PD-L1 in pancreatic cancer. By targeting αvβ3, DL-N2 disrupts this signaling axis, thereby enhancing the anti-proliferative effects of gefitinib and mitigating immune checkpoint expression. These findings validate our in-silico predictions of ITGAV/ITGB3–EGFR co-activation and establish integrin αvβ3 as a central.

DL-N2 and gefitinib inhibited the ERK1/2 phosphorylation (Fig. 12) synergistically. These findings complement our earlier observations that DL-N2 reduces EGFR phosphorylation, establishing a consistent biological narrative: integrin αvβ3 is a central regulator of growth, survival, and drug response in pancreatic cancer, and its targeting offers a dual benefit of direct anti-tumor activity and enhanced therapeutic efficacy.

Our findings demonstrate that DL‑N2, either alone or in combination with gefitinib, effectively suppresses the migratory capacity of pancreatic cancer cells (Figs. 13 and 14). Both wound healing and Transwell assays consistently showed that the combination therapy exerted a more pronounced inhibitory effect than either monotherapy, highlighting a potential synergistic interaction. Mechanistically, DL‑N2 downregulated MMP 9 and attenuated the expression of pro‑angiogenic factors, such as bFGF2 and VEGF‑α (Fig. 11), thereby counteracting extracellular matrix remodeling and angiogenic signaling. Importantly, while monotherapy with DL‑N2 or gefitinib induced compensatory upregulation of bFGF2 and VEGF‑α in AsPC‑1 cells, their combined treatment reversed this effect, suggesting that αvβ3 blockade not only enhances the anti‑migratory activity of EGFR inhibition but also mitigates adaptive pro‑angiogenic responses. Collectively, these results support the therapeutic potential of dual targeting strategies to overcome resistance mechanisms and achieve more durable suppression of pancreatic cancer progression.

The results provide functional validation of our computational predictions that ITGAV/ITGB3 cooperates with EGFR to drive proliferation and therapeutic resistance in PDAC. By co-targeting these pathways with DL-N2 and an EGFR inhibitor, we successfully disrupted integrin αvβ3 signaling, thereby potentiating the overall anti-cancer.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study (Fig. 15) establishes integrin αvβ3 as a pivotal therapeutic checkpoint Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), coordinating oncogenic signaling, stromal remodeling, and immune evasion. By integrating single-cell transcriptomic profiling with experimental validation, we demonstrate that integrin αvβ3 is selectively overexpressed in the tumor compartment and functionally interacts with EGFR to drive disease progression. Blockade of this axis with DL-N2 significantly inhibited both basal and EGF-driven proliferation, suppressed angiogenic mediators, and reduced PD-L1 expression, effectively disrupting the synergy between intrinsic oncogenic programs and the extrinsic microenvironment. Furthermore, DL-N2 demonstrated potent synergy with gefitinib and maintained cytotoxic efficacy as a doxorubicin conjugate, even in gemcitabine-resistant models. Together, these findings highlight integrinαvβ3 as a master regulator of the pancreatic tumor ecosystem and establish DL-N2 as a versatile therapeutic platform. Dual inhibition of integrin αvβ3 and EGFR represents a rational strategy to overcome drug resistance and improve outcomes in this recalcitrant malignancy.

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: While our study provides a comprehensive look at integrin αvβ3 through multi-omics and functional assays, several limitations remain. First, while we utilized single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to clarify cellular localization and transcriptomic shifts, we did not perform spatial multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC). Although our current data strongly support the observed phenotypic changes, future studies employing mIHC would provide deeper insights into the precise spatial architecture of these protein-level interactions within the complex PAAD stroma. Second, while our transcriptomic analysis focused on the most relevant signaling hubs, we did not include comprehensive bulk RNA-seq for every experimental condition, as we focused on validated protein-level outcomes and targeted gene expression. Third, our functional validation was primarily conducted in vitro; while we utilized gemcitabine-resistant models to enhance clinical relevance, these systems do not fully replicate the dense desmoplastic reaction of human tumors. Consequently, the observed suppression of PD-L1 by DL-N2 requires further validation in immunocompetent, syngeneic mouse models to confirm its impact on immune infiltration. Finally, while the DL-N2–doxorubicin conjugate shows promise, detailed pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles are necessary before clinical translation. Addressing these areas, alongside the interplay between integrin αvβ3 and KRAS signaling, will be the focus of our future research.
